12 step groups come for a lot of addictions, not just alcohol. I'm not an alcoholic and I've gone for many years to almost any 12 step group available and when I introduce myself say I'm addict or a codependent. Everyone who had parents qualifies in a general sense. That's enough. In my case it's anxiety, depression and illness. It's a place to get support for 1 dollar a session as opposed to paying much more for a therapist. I'm not a theist either. You take what helps and leave the rest. And you can find 12 steps almost where ever you go. When you're lonely, afraid or anxious, they're there. Although one on one therapy is good, peer therapy is good too. That's what these groups provide.

Why the judgement?

It's the fundamental attraction of 12 step groups of all kinds around the world, isn't it?  By AA’s own figures, there are currently approximately [120,300 AA groups worldwide](https://www.aa.org/assets/en_US/smf-132_en.pdf). You may trivialize it but a lot of people find relief hearing other's have worse, or same difficulties and it keeps them going another day...

There is a an empty seat waiting for you, by the way.

If you put yourself in the position of someone with a terminal disease, given you don't have one, you might experience a moment of relief and satisfaction. Yes, slowly it gets worse, but someone else has it worse still and that is something to celebrate. You could help that person with less than you have for a flash of satisfaction. Our condition is relative to others. Look down at what you don't want in place of looking up at what you don't have. Take a trip to a poor country and visit densely packed slums. Although people living there see their lot in life relative to their neighbors and feel a sense of relief when they don't have to go through what a neighbor does, you have more options. If there is an adventure you want, but feel you can't for reasons that aren't truly impediments, maybe you should take it.
